newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 15.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 15.

text.p: THE DOMINION

NZ First leader Winston Peters revealed on Thursday that alternative policy programmes for both a National-lead and a Labour-led coalition had been drawn up and were being costed by his party. Coalition talks were postponed on Thursday till late in the day for what Peters's office described as a crucial meeting with the party's unidentified economic advisers, and for a meeting with Reserve Bank governor Don Brash. NZ First is drawing up full policy programmes in parallel with both parties, will all parties hoping for an announcement by the end of the month on which party NZ First plans to go into government with.
Page 1.

Telecom Corporation's share price rose to a record high of $7.75 on Thursday before the company announced it would buy back $1 billion of shares from shareholders in the coming year. The share price had risen recently on rumours that the company might buy back as much as $1.5 billion of shares. The lower-than-expected figure, announced Thursday afternoon, caused the share price to fade quickly, ending the day at $7.47. Telecom also announced a $360.9 million after-tax profit for the six months to September 30, which was at the lower end of
expectations. Page 1.

The Government planned to spend up to $30 million more than previously proposed on a new building for cabinet ministers and other MPs next to the Parliament Building, Deputy Prime Minister Don McKinnon said on Thursday. Page 1.

Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen, who is expected to be finance minister if Labour and NZ First form a coalition government, on Thursday called on the Reserve Bank to say it would allow the exchange rate to fall. The level of the dollar,

which is at nearly an eight-year high against the United States dollar, has led to repeated calls to the central bank from exporters and some sides of the political spectrum who want intervention to being the dollar down. Cullen said New Zealand had "the most unbalanced mix of exchange rates, interest rates, fiscal surpluses and current account deficits in the developed world". Page 2.

The United Nations General Assembly had voted to accept a New Zealand co-sponsored resolution promoting the establishment of a nuclear weapon-free Southern Hemisphere, Disarmament Minister Doug Graham said on Thursday. Page 2.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger has announced plans for a whistle-stop trip to Manila later this month, intending to be out of the country as short a time as possible as coalition talks near a conclusion. Bolger will be away three nights and will spend only one night on the ground attending the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders forum. Page 2.
Agriculture Minister Lockwood Smith believes the world food summit in Rome has stayed in step with New Zealand's views on free trade in agriculture. Page 2.

Increases in workers' productivity has slumped since the Employment Contracts Act was introduced in 1992, according to research by Victoria University economist Bryan Philpott. Philpott said from 1992 labour productivity, which measures output per worker, grew on average by only 0.7 percent each year. That was down on annual growth of 1.5 percent for the
years from 1984 till 1992. Page 2.

Registered unemployed had fallen slightly, Employment Minister Wyatt Creech said on Thursday. Employment Service statistics issued on Thursday show 153,906 people on the register, a drop of 227 since last month. Page 2.

Telecom Corporation posted a $360.9 million after-tax profit for the six months to September 30, up 6.8 percent on the previous year. Telecom also announced plans for a $1 billion share buyback. A second-quarter fully imputed dividend of 9.5

cents a share will be paid, up from 8.5 cents in the same quarter last year. But credit ratings agency Standard and Poor's put Telecom on credit watch with "negative implications" while it awaits details on the proposed share buyback. Page 13.

A high-powered World Bank conference aimed at helping Asian and Latin American governments corporatise and privatise state assets using New Zealand's experience will be held in Wellington in December. The wide-ranging agenda with a who's who of business and government and World Bank sponsorship indicates how highly the bank regards New Zealand's
corporatisation-privatisation programme as a model for others. Page 13.

Heinz-Wattie on Thursday confirmed it was reviewing the future of Tip Top Icecream and Tegel Foods as part of a worldwide review of non-core businesses and that a sale of the familiar kiwi brands was one option. However, a spokesman said no decision had been made to sell the brands. Page 16.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

Auckland Mayor Les Mills and his allies defied their critics to push on with the controversial Britomart development they claim will transform downtown Auckland. After two years of furious debate, Auckland City councillors on Thursday night faced a rowdy public meeting largely opposed to the $1.5 billion development and voted by 16-7 in favour. The vote flew in the face of intense lobbying by critics, including transport operators and the business community, for a rethink of the project, which includes an underground transport centre.

Senior cabinet ministers were summoned to the Prime Minister's office on Thursday to hammer out the bottom line that National should take on supperannuation in coalition talks with NZ First. It is understood cabinet ministers did not reach a decision by the time talks resumed with NZ First on Thursday. Ministers are still debating how far they should compromise on what is becoming the critical issue in the negotiations.

NZ First has costed alternative programmes featuring both National and Labour, indicating it should be in a position to strike a deal before Parliament meets next month. However, NZ First leader Winston Peters indicated the work was not completed and there was still room for movement. He made the comments after an hour-long meeting on Thursday with Reserve Bank governor Don Brash. It is believed Peters wanted to consult Brash on the fiscal sustainability and implications for the dollar of the various possibilities on the coalition menu. Peters postponed talks with National and Labour until later on Thursday evening so he could hold two meetings, one with Brash
and one with NZ First's independent economic advisers.

Telecom Corporation on Thursday became the first major New Zealand corporate to announce plans for a share buyback. Other things being equal, buying back shares increases the value of the remaining shares. It would also reduce Telecom's cost of capital because it would have less equity and more debt, which is cheaper. In all Telecom intends to spend $1 billion. For every share it buys on-market, it will buy one back off-market from its major shareholders, Bell Atlantic and Ameritech.

The Telecom profit juggernaut slowed during the September quarter as the economy cooled and competition stayed hot. Net profit for the half-year was $306.9 million, 6.8 percent ahead of the saem period last year. It would have been 10.7 percent up, had it not been for the $22.5 million loss returned by the Pacific Star operation in Australia. But those numbers mask a slowdown in revenue growth between the first and second quarter, which chief executive Roderick Deane blamed on market-driven price reductions and the slower growth of the New Zealand economy.

The continuing fallout from Telcom's abortive attempt to buy a stake in Sky Network television drew some cross words from the Telecom chief executive Roderick Deane on Thursday. Although Telcom has abandoned the planned acquisition and an associated agreement on content for its fledgling cable telvision network, First Media, litigation brought by Clear Communications continues and has been widened.
Affco boosted its operating profit by 9.5 percent to to $26.5 million in the September year, but warned that earnings were unlikely to exceed that figure in 1997.
